# Configuration

*1 of 65 rules below are **designed** rather than shipped, and are marked where they appear.*

<a id="config-the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml"></a>

## The configuration file is `nvs.toml`, and it is TOML

`rule:config/the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml`

The server configuration is a TOML file named `nvs.toml`, read into the directive registry through the
`toml` crate and `serde` — at boot, and again on each reload, which parses and validates a whole
replacement before publishing it and leaves the running configuration untouched if any part fails.
Pure Rust, no C, and no new dependency class: Cargo's own manifests are TOML.

INI does not survive an argument. It has no specification — every parser
disagrees on comment markers, quoting, nesting and what a duplicate key means — and it has one value
type, string, which is the defect the language itself rejects. TOML has a boolean, an integer, an
array and an array of tables, and an editor already validates it. The configuration was never all
strings: "no ceiling", a list of debug modes, a list of capability roots and an extension with its hash
pin are a boolean, two arrays and a repeated record, and each would otherwise be a mini-grammar to
specify, parse, fuzz and diagnose. With TOML the implementation carries no dialect parser, no comma or
`PATH` splitter and no `on`/`off`/`yes`/`no` table, and a parse error names a line. The familiarity INI
offers is thin: almost no directive shares a key name with `php.ini`, so no PHP file was ever
copy-pastable, and the sectioned key/value shape that does transfer is TOML's too.

`nvs.toml` names the **root of a tree**, not the whole configuration:
[`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults) says where that root is found
and [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir) how it pulls in more. Every file in the tree is written
in this syntax, and [`config/every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added`](config.md#config-every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added) lists the blocks.

The `[limits]`/`[limits.hard]` layout is the changeability model's
([`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes)); this rule gives it only its syntax.

- **Memory:** nothing on the request path. The parse runs at boot and on each reload, over files
  measured in kilobytes, and never per request or from a request-serving core; what a live snapshot
  holds is [`config/the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot`](config.md#config-the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot)'s to state.

**Declined:**
- **INI.** No specification, one value type, four directives that would encode non-strings as strings,
  a `:`-joined root list that cannot spell a Windows path, and a dialect Novis would own forever.
- **YAML.** Indentation-significant, with a parser-CVE record and a value whose *type* depends on how it
  was typed (`no` as `false`, a version number as a float), in the root-owned file that grants
  capabilities.
- **JSON or JSONC.** JSON has no comments, in a file whose main job is recording why an operator chose a
  number; JSONC is one non-standard extension, which brings back the missing specification.
- **KDL, RON or HCL.** An operator meets the format for the first time and the editor does not validate
  it, and nothing any of them offers is reachable at this file's size.
- **Dhall, or configuration written in Novis.** Either makes the configuration a program, reopening the
  door [`security/closed-doors`](security.md#security-closed-doors) closed on `eval` in the one root-owned file read before any sandbox
  exists.
- **`${ENV_VAR}` interpolation in a value.** It makes the configuration compute, the same door Dhall
  reopens. The run mode is never read from the environment
  ([`config/no-environment-variable-selects-the-mode`](config.md#config-no-environment-variable-selects-the-mode)), and an inherited, unaudited namespace is no
  source for the file that grants capabilities. A secret arrives as a file instead
  ([`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value)).
- **Accepting both `.ini` and `.toml`.** Two formats to specify, parse and test, and a deployment that
  holds both with no answer for which wins; nothing in Novis gets a second syntax.

<sub>See also [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults), [`config/lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables`](config.md#config-lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables), [`config/three-changeability-classes`](config.md#config-three-changeability-classes), [`config/the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot`](config.md#config-the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot).</sub>

<a id="config-a-size-or-duration-is-a-quoted-string-with-its-suffix"></a>

## A size or a duration is a quoted string carrying its suffix, a count is an integer, and `false` removes a ceiling

`rule:config/a-size-or-duration-is-a-quoted-string-with-its-suffix`

A size or a duration is written as a **quoted string carrying its suffix** — `memory = "128M"`,
`cpu_time = "5s"` — never as a bare integer of implied units. The suffix is what makes the file readable
at a glance, and the parser for it has to exist anyway for `Core\Config::set("memory", "512M")`
([`config/one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set`](config.md#config-one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set)). A count, such as `max_tasks = 64`, is an
ordinary integer.

"No ceiling" is a boolean, and TOML has one: `[limits.hard] memory = false` removes the ceiling, and
`memory = "2G"` enforces it. There is no magic word `off`.

Every size suffix names the same binary multiple and every duration suffix the same span of
nanoseconds wherever the value is spelled, and one limit has one unit in every block that carries it —
`[limits]`, `[limits.hard]`, `[app.limits]` and `[app.limits.hard]` agree on what `memory` measures.

**Declined:**
- **Bare integers of implied units (`memory = 134217728`).** It saves no parser, since
  `Core\Config::set` needs the suffix parser anyway, and it leaves a file nobody can edit with
  confidence.
- **A magic word such as `off` for "no ceiling".** TOML has a boolean, and a word table is one more
  grammar to specify ([`config/the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml`](config.md#config-the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml)).

<sub>See also [`config/one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set`](config.md#config-one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set).</sub>

<a id="config-lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables"></a>

## A list is a TOML array, a repeated record is an array of tables, and a dotted key is table nesting

`rule:config/lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables`

A directive holding several values is a TOML array, and a directive that is a repeated record with
more than one field is an array of tables:

```toml
[debug]
mode = ["coverage", "branch"]                 # [] is off

[capabilities]
script.spawn = ["/srv/www/jobs", "C:\\srv\\jobs"]

[[extension]]
path   = "image.nvsx"
sha256 = "…"
```

Nothing is a comma-joined or `PATH`-joined string. The `:`-joined root list could not spell a Windows
absolute path at all, since every one contains the separator, and the extension hash pin gets a shape
instead of a convention — which matters because that pin is what accepting a precompiled binary rests
on.

A capability's name is dotted, and a dotted TOML key *is* table nesting: `script.spawn` under
`[capabilities]` and a `[capabilities.script]` block with a `spawn` key are the same thing, and the
registry names the directive by its full dotted path either way. Neither spelling needs quoting.

Across files the two shapes behave differently, which is
[`config/a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends`](config.md#config-a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends).

Array-of-tables syntax gets noisy past two levels of nesting, and a block layout that would need a
third is flattened rather than nested deeper.

<sub>See also [`config/a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends`](config.md#config-a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends), [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir).</sub>

<a id="config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one"></a>

## A duplicate key is an error, and so is an unknown one — per file

`rule:config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`

The same key set twice in one file is refused (`E0604`), and so is a key the registry does not know
(`E0601`) — both name the file and the line. In a root-owned file where one table grants
capabilities, a line silently overridden by a later copy of itself is a security-relevant failure that
costs nothing to refuse, and a typo'd `capabilties` must fail at boot rather than read as "granted
nothing". A typo'd block header is refused the same way and claims no block. Both are `serde`'s own
behaviour with `deny_unknown_fields`; neither is new machinery.

**One exception: an unknown header with nothing under it is a warning (`W1024`), not `E0601`.** A
plain `[table]` header the typed tree has no block for, with no key under it at any depth, is removed
from its file before the file is typed, and the warning names the header, the file and the line. An
empty header sets nothing, so letting it through loses none of what the refusal protects: there is no
value to misread as "granted nothing". What it buys is that a file written for a release that had the
block, with every key commented out, still starts after the block is folded into another or removed.
Anything under the header — a key, a sub-table with a key, `name = {}` — keeps it `E0601`, and so does
an empty `[[entry]]` of an unknown array, because writing an entry states that it exists. An empty
header the tree *does* know is no block at all, the same as a file that never wrote it, and raises no
warning. `nvs_config::file::parse_with_warnings` is the one place this runs; it costs nothing on a
file that types first time.

**The four open blocks are not an exception to the refusal.** `[settings]`, `[secrets]`,
`[app.settings]` and `[app.secrets]` take any key that is a plain name, because the operator names
it ([`config/settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values`](config.md#config-settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values)). What a closed block's field set
refuses, their own per-file check refuses instead, with the line: a key that is not a plain name, a
date or time, a secret that is not a string. A key no program reads is `nvs config check`'s warning
and not a refusal, because a program the tree does not name may read it.

On a reload the same diagnostic refuses the swap and the previous snapshot keeps serving, so a typo is
never published to a running server either.

**Both refusals are per file.** Across an `[[include]]` the same key set twice is not a duplicate but
an override, which [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded) allows on condition that it
is reported with both origins. The property protected is that no assignment is *silently* shadowed;
inside one file the only way to hold it is to refuse, and an included file is refused inside exactly as
the root is.

<sub>See also [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded), [`config/the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml`](config.md#config-the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml), [`config/the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot`](config.md#config-the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot).</sub>

<a id="config-every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added"></a>

## The block roster is closed, and each block's directives are argued by the rule that adds it

`rule:config/every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added`

The set of top-level blocks is closed, and the typed tree refuses any other with the unknown-key
diagnostic ([`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one)). That rule's one
exception holds here too: an unknown header with nothing under it is ignored with a warning. The
format rule owns
only the *syntax*; every block's directives, defaults and changeability class are argued by the rule
that adds the block, so a reader of `nvs.toml` has one place to start.

**Four blocks are open**: `[settings]`, `[secrets]`, `[app.settings]` and `[app.secrets]` take keys
the operator names. Every other block's keys are closed.


| Block | Argued by |
|---|---|
| `[[include]]` | [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir) |
| `[[app]]` | [`config/an-application-is-its-entry-file-path`](config.md#config-an-application-is-its-entry-file-path) |
| `[limits]`, `[limits.hard]`, `[capabilities]` | the changeability model and the capability rules |
| `[mode]` | the run-mode rules |
| `[[extension]]` | the extension system |
| `[debug]` | [`testing/debug-mode-directive`](testing.md#testing-debug-mode-directive) |
| `[log]`, `[http.errors]` | [`errors/log-level`](errors.md#errors-log-level), [`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor) |
| `[errors]` | [`errors/a-use-of-deprecated-code-may-log-or-throw`](errors.md#errors-a-use-of-deprecated-code-may-log-or-throw) |
| `[db.<name>]` | [`core-classes/db-connection-is-named`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-connection-is-named) |
| `[deferred]` | [`concurrency/deferred-is-bounded-by-two-directives`](concurrency.md#concurrency-deferred-is-bounded-by-two-directives) |
| `[[schedule]]`, `[queue]` | the scheduled-work rules, [`core-classes/queue-storage-is-a-table`](core-classes.md#core-classes-queue-storage-is-a-table) |
| `[http.headers]`, `[http.cors]`, `[http.cookies]`, `[http.client]` | the safe-defaults rules |
| `[metrics]`, `[trace]` | the observability rules |
| `[server]`, `[[server.mount]]` | [`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount) |
| `[cache]`, `[opcache]` | the artifact cache and hot reload rules |
| `[image]` | [`core-classes/image-pipeline`](core-classes.md#core-classes-image-pipeline) |
| `[io]` | [`core-classes/temporary-dir-sweep`](core-classes.md#core-classes-temporary-dir-sweep) |
| `[mail.<name>]`, `[storage.<name>]` | [`programs/framework-core-half`](programs.md#programs-framework-core-half) |
| `[session]` | [`http-server/session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-session-backend-is-shared-or-db-and-memory-is-refused-at-boot) |
| `[app.log]` | [`errors/handler-script`](errors.md#errors-handler-script) |
| `[settings]`, `[secrets]`, `[app.settings]`, `[app.secrets]` | [`config/settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values`](config.md#config-settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values) |

`[[schedule]]`, like `[[extension]]`, is an array of tables because it is a repeated record with
several fields.

<a id="config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest"></a>

## `nvs.toml` is a deployment file, never a project manifest, and it is never found by walking up

`rule:config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`

`nvs.toml` is a root-owned deployment file. It is **never searched for by walking up from a source
file**, it holds no source-tree state, and an `[autoload]` table is refused as an unknown key for the
reason [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload) gives: the rejection of "a manifest found by walking up from
the entry file" stands, and it is about discovery and lifetime rather than syntax. The autoload map is
a property of the source tree, while `nvs.toml` is deployment state: it is absent from
`nvs build --compile` and from an editor's `nvs check`, and a map in it would make one source tree
behave differently under two hosts, which the artifact cache would then have to key on. Sharing an extension
with `Cargo.toml` is not a collision; the name, the location and the owner all differ. A package may
not hold an `nvs.toml` ([`packaging/a-package-cannot-reach-its-host`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-cannot-reach-its-host)), and a working directory is
not a package: committing a development `nvs.toml` to a project is fine, and deploying it is what
`--config` is for.

Where the file *is* found is [`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults):
a `--config` list, else `./nvs.toml` in exactly one directory, else the data folder's `nvs.toml`. That
single-directory step is deliberately one step short of a walk, and the step is not taken. The data
folder's file is Novis's own default, one per data folder and not per project. What makes a file in a
working directory safe to read there is [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), the resolved
absolute path announced at boot, and the installer storing an absolute `--config` for every service.

<sub>See also [`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload).</sub>

<a id="config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults"></a>

## The root of the tree is every `--config` in order, else `./nvs.toml`, else the data folder's `nvs.toml`, else the shipped defaults

`rule:config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`

Four steps, first hit wins:

1. Every `--config <path>`, in the order given. The flag is **repeatable**, and the files form an
   ordered list merged exactly as an include list is. A `--config` naming a file that does not exist
   is always a hard refusal — optionality is a property a file declares about *its* includes, never
   something argv can assert.
2. `./nvs.toml` — **exactly one directory, never a walk upward.** Any explicit `--config` disables this
   step and the next entirely, so an operator naming files never gets a surprise merge with whatever is
   in the working directory or the data folder, even if every named file turns out to be missing.
3. `nvs.toml` in the **data folder** — `.nvsdata` beside the running binary, or the folder the global
   `--data` flag names — if it exists. A process with no usable data folder skips this step. The file
   Novis writes there starts with a line naming its version and a hash of the rest, and before the
   first lookup reads it, an unedited one another version wrote is replaced with this version's
   template; a file without the line or with another hash is never touched, and a refresh that cannot
   write reads the file as it is.
4. Otherwise the shipped defaults
   ([`config/no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration`](config.md#config-no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration)). A **project command** — `run`,
   `serve`, `test`, `build`, `check` and `dap` — first writes the shipped default file as the data folder's
   `nvs.toml`, the file step 3 looks for, and then reads it. Every key in it is commented out, so it
   resolves to exactly the shipped defaults. `--no-init`, or `NOVIS_NO_INIT` set to any value, turns
   that one write off; the data folder itself is still created. A write the folder refuses is no
   error: the run continues on the shipped defaults.

**Novis never writes `./nvs.toml` on its own.** The working directory holds a file only when somebody
put it there, or asked `nvs init` to write it. The language server's per-document lookup takes the
same four steps with the document's folder in place of the working directory. `nvs config check` and
`nvs config dump` take the `--config` list positionally.

There is no platform path and no build-time path. The data folder is the one lookup beside the binary:
it is a folder Novis creates private to its account ([`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)),
it comes after both explicit steps, and a deployment that wants a file of its own names it with
`--config` or moves the folder with `--data`.

The data folder is beside the file the binary really is: the running binary's path is canonicalized,
so a binary reached through a link uses the folder beside its target. An unedited template is
refreshed because a block a later version removes would otherwise make every command of that version
stop on the file an older one wrote. The cost is usability: a binary in a directory its account cannot
write, such as a packaged `/usr/bin/nvs` run by an ordinary user, finds no usable default folder,
prints the one warning, and runs without a compile cache until `--data` names a folder. One binary
serving several deployments shares one default folder, so a deployment that wants its own passes
`--config` or `--data`, and a service always stores one.

- **Memory:** none. Locating the folder is one canonicalization per process, and preparing it is one
  create attempt per folder at startup.

What makes the working-directory step safe is [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), the
announced path ([`config/the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored`](config.md#config-the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored)) and an installer that always
stores an absolute `--config` for a service ([`packaging/the-installer-is-a-sink`](packaging.md#packaging-the-installer-is-a-sink)). What survives
is one narrow case — an interactive `nvs serve` in a directory the runtime account can write — stated
rather than defended: an operator who wants it closed passes `--config`. If the announced path shows
`./nvs.toml` being read in production, the answer is to confine the working-directory step to the
commands attached to a terminal, not to remove it.

**Declined:**
- **A platform default path, such as `/etc/nvs/nvs.toml`.** A deployment that wants a fixed path runs
  under a service manager, and the installer stores an absolute `--config` for it anyway
  ([`packaging/the-installer-is-a-sink`](packaging.md#packaging-the-installer-is-a-sink)).
- **A path built into the binary at compile time**, as nginx's `--conf-path` is. It is one more
  resolution step for a case `--config` already covers.
- **Walking up from the working directory or the entry file.** The single-directory step stops one
  step short of a walk ([`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest)).
- **Per-platform locations for Novis's own files**, such as a cache under the user's local application
  data and a temporary root in the system temporary directory. They are several places an operator has
  to know, one of them shared with every other program on the host.
- **A data folder under the user's profile.** It moves with the account, not with the binary, so two
  installed versions or a portable copy would share it, and a service account's profile is a place
  nobody looks.

<sub>See also [`config/no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration`](config.md#config-no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration), [`config/the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored`](config.md#config-the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored), [`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest), [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir).</sub>

<a id="config-no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration"></a>

## A host with no configuration file runs on the shipped defaults, which are a complete configuration and not an error

`rule:config/no-configuration-file-is-a-complete-configuration`

When no `--config` is given and neither `./nvs.toml` nor the data folder's `nvs.toml` exists, the host
runs on the **shipped defaults**, and
those are a complete and valid configuration rather than a failure to find one: every capability at
its default, `[mode] default = "production"`, and every limit at its documented default. The boot log says
so in one line. They stay the configuration whenever a project command could not write the data
folder's `nvs.toml` ([`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults)).

**An unwritten `[limits] memory` is 128 MiB, for every kind of run.** **An unwritten `cpu_time` is 30
seconds for server work** — a request, a connection, a scheduled run, a queued job and every isolate
in their trees — **and no ceiling for `nvs run`, a `#[Command]` method and `nvs test`**, as a CLI
program has no execution-time limit in PHP either. `wall_time` has no default. `false` written for
either key is no ceiling, and the default is what a written `false` is distinguished from. A context
that was handed no configuration at all takes neither default: it has no tree to read one from.

**An unwritten `[limits.hard]` key is the `[limits]` value the run started with** — the written one
after `[app.limits]` folded into it, or the default above — so a program narrows its own limit with
`Core\Config::set` and raises it only once the operator writes a ceiling above the start
([`config/ceilings-are-their-own-directives`](config.md#config-ceilings-are-their-own-directives)). Under `nvs run` an unwritten `cpu_time` has no
start value, so nothing bounds a set of it either. **An unwritten `[limits.hard] memory` is no ceiling
on a CLI run**, so a CLI program's own code raises its memory limit freely; in server work it is the
start value, as every other key is.

**Every built-in default has one home: the config crate's table of defaults.** Each key the shipped
`nvs.toml` marks `# default` has its value there, and every piece of code that enforces the value
reads it from there — the runtime, the `Core\Config::set` bound and admission among them. A test holds every `# default` line of the shipped file to the table, so the file and the code
cannot disagree. A default that is not one value is computed when it is read: `cpu_time` by the kind
of run, the mode table's rows by the mode in force, `[server] dispatch`, `static` and
`[opcache] settle` by the mode the run started in, `[mode] ceiling` as that mode, and
`[server] workers` as this machine's cores.

- **Memory:** up to 128 MiB per request in flight where no `[limits] memory` is written. That is a
  request's ceiling and not what it is assumed to hold: admission counts what requests hold and
  leaves room for one more to reach the cap ([`http-server/admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number`](http-server.md#http-server-admission-is-arithmetic-not-a-number)).
  It is spent to buy **Security and request isolation**: a host nobody configured can no longer be
  exhausted by one request.

Every reader has to answer on such a host, and none of them throws, because "no configuration file
anywhere" is a valid host and a program has to be able to ask on one. **`Core\Config::get` and `all`
give the value in force**: what the request set, then a secret, then what the file wrote, then the
built-in default, rendered the way the shipped file writes it (`128M`, `30s`, `1000000`). A key with
no default (`wall_time`) is `null`, and so is a key whose default is nothing for this run
(`cpu_time` under `nvs run`). An unwritten `[log] target` is `null` too, because it is not one
destination: a `Core\Log::write` record is the program's output and a floor record goes to stderr
([`errors/engine-floor`](errors.md#errors-engine-floor)). A default inside a named block (`[db.<name>]`) is in force only where
that block is written. `set` and `restore` behave as on any host: `set` is bounded as above, and
`restore` brings back the written value or the default. A context that was handed no configuration
at all — a test context, an embedder that has not built a snapshot — has no tree and no defaults:
`get` is `null`, `all` is empty, `set` is `false` and `restore` does nothing.

**An unwritten `fs.read` or `fs.write` is every path on a CLI run.** In server work an unwritten
`fs.read` is the app folder, less every path with a component below it that starts with `.` (`.env`,
`.git/config`) and every file named `nvs.toml`, and an unwritten `fs.write` is the directories
`Core\IO::temporaryDir` made for this context, which it also reads. A written key replaces its
default whole, so `read = []` reads nothing and leaves writing at its default. An unwritten
`net.connect` is every public host on both run kinds, and an unwritten `net.internal` is loopback on
a CLI run and in a run that started in `development` ([`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy),
[`config/a-startup-default-is-never-flipped`](config.md#config-a-startup-default-is-never-flipped)). An unwritten `process.exec` is every program on a
CLI run and none in server work ([`security/process-exec-capability`](security.md#security-process-exec-capability)), and an unwritten
`script.spawn` is the app folder on both, less its temporary directories
([`security/script-spawn-capability`](security.md#security-script-spawn-capability)). Every other capability defaults to nothing
([`security/capability-question-is-grant-and-scope`](security.md#security-capability-question-is-grant-and-scope)). The defaults are the application's own:
a package is checked against its own grant line alone
([`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time)). `nvs serve`
names, in one boot line per app folder whose tree writes no `fs.read`, the folder its requests read.

- **Memory:** the app folder is one path per context, and the temporary directories are the list
  the context already keeps for its sweep ([`core-classes/temporary-dir-sweep`](core-classes.md#core-classes-temporary-dir-sweep)). It buys
  **Simplicity**: a first program reads and writes its files with no `nvs.toml`, while a server
  never writes beside code it would run, never reads its own secrets, and one request cannot reach
  another's directory.

The one distinction the shipped defaults keep is between *no tree* and *a tree that grants nothing*:
a program checked outside any project root has no configuration to be measured against, while a tree
that was read and writes a capability's key as `[]` is an operator's written `no`. A context handed
no configuration at all grants nothing. The offline audit reports the first as a tree of zero files.

**A `[block]` header with no key under it says nothing, and the resolver drops it before the tree is
typed**, at any depth and for a named block as much as a fixed one: `[metrics]` alone is no
`[metrics]`, and `[db.main]` alone names no connection. No reader of a block is ever handed one that
is present and empty, so none has to decide what that would mean. That is what lets the shipped file
carry its headers live — setting a key there is removing one `#` — and still resolve to exactly what
no file resolves to. An `[[entry]]` is the exception, because writing one says the entry exists: an
`[[app]]` with no path is refused rather than skipped, and the shipped file keeps every `[[entry]]`
header, and the tables belonging to one, commented out — and the two `pool` tables under `[db]`,
each of which is the same TOML key as the `pool = false` beside it and cannot be live with it.
`bun nv directives
--check-template` refuses a key left under a commented-out header when the live header above it has
a key of the same name, which is the one arrangement where uncommenting the key alone would be
accepted into the wrong block.

**Declined:**
- **A default for a grant that turns a check off or reaches what an operator has to name.**
  `net.listen`, the four `tls.*` relaxations, `ldap.cleartext`, `net.downgrade`, `db.schema`,
  `queue.purge`, `cache.shared`, `mail.send`, every `debug.*` grant and the named `[db.*]` and
  `[ldap.*]` blocks keep no default, and so do CORS, the cookie attributes and the security headers.
  Each one either weakens a protection the program cannot see, or reaches a service only the
  operator knows, so a default would be a guess with the operator's authority.
- **A writable `storage/` folder in server work.** A written upload could land beside code the
  default `script.spawn` would run. A server writes only its own temporary directories until a line
  says where else.
- **Loopback in production server work.** [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy) records why.

<sub>See also [`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults), [`config/ini-set-is-core-config-set`](config.md#config-ini-set-is-core-config-set), [`config/two-modes-and-the-default-is-production`](config.md#config-two-modes-and-the-default-is-production).</sub>

<a id="config-the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored"></a>

## The resolved root is stored once at boot as the absolute path it was given, announced with every file it reached, and resolved again through its links on reload

`rule:config/the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored`

Whichever step won is **stored once, at boot, as the absolute path it was given, never its
canonical path**. A reload resolves that stored path again, through its links, and never re-resolves
the working directory or the data folder. So a swapped `current` link or a changed Kubernetes
ConfigMap is read by the next reload without a restart, a deployment that replaced its directory
under a running process reloads the file the operator can see rather than an unlinked inode, and a
`nvs.toml` that appears in the working directory later is not read until the next boot. A boot on
the shipped defaults reloads the shipped defaults. The configuration check stats each stored root
as given, beside the files the tree reached, and a stamp carries the file's identity, so a link that
points at a new file with the same time and size is still noticed. Because the link decides the
file, the directory that holds each link on the stored path is ownership-checked like the file's own
([`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)), at boot and on every reload.

`nvs serve` prints the root as it was found, the path it was read from, and every file the tree
reached, on standard error before it binds:

```console
$ nvs serve
info: configuration ./nvs.toml -> /srv/www/app/nvs.toml
info: resolved from 3 files
info:   /srv/www/app/nvs.toml
info:   /srv/www/app/conf.d/10-limits.toml
info:   /etc/nvs/local.toml
```

The announcement is half of what makes the two implicit steps of
[`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults) safe — the working directory's
`nvs.toml` and the data folder's: reading the wrong file is visible in one line rather than silent.
When no step finds a file, `info: configuration: no file was found, so the shipped defaults apply`
is printed instead. When step 4's write into the data folder declines, its reason is one more `info:`
line ahead of that one. Other commands print none of these, so `nvs run`'s standard error stays the
program's own.

The stored roots are `crates/nvs-cli/src/config.rs`'s `Root`, and a reload resolves them through
`stored_set`.

<sub>See also [`config/the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults`](config.md#config-the-root-is-config-else-nvs-toml-else-the-shipped-defaults), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), [`config/the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot`](config.md#config-the-config-is-an-immutable-snapshot).</sub>

<a id="config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir"></a>

## `[[include]]` takes a `path` or a `dir`, never both and never neither, and a `dir` is not a glob

`rule:config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`

`[[include]]` is a top-level array of tables, and an entry carries `path` **or** `dir`, never both and
never neither:

```toml
[[include]]
path = "conf.d/production.toml"

[[include]]
dir = "conf.d"                    # every *.toml directly inside, ascending by filename

[[include]]
path = "/etc/nvs/local.toml"
optional = true                   # absent is fine
```

`dir` is **not** a glob. It reads every `*.toml` directly inside that directory, in ascending byte
order of filename, without recursing, and the order is mandated rather than inherited from `readdir`
because [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded) makes order decide the answer — a
capability grant settled by directory-entry order is not a design. A pattern language is refused for
the same reason INI was: a grammar to specify, fuzz and diagnose for a feature whose whole job is
"read this directory".

An `[[include]]` inside an included file is ordinary
([`config/an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight`](config.md#config-an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight)), and an included file is
a configuration file in every other respect: unknown and duplicate keys are refused inside it exactly
as in the root, its paths resolve against its own directory, and it must pass
[`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary). What `optional` does and does not cover is
[`config/optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory`](config.md#config-optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory).

**Declined:**
- **A `sha256` pin on an `[[include]]`**, as `[[extension]]` has. The pin exists on an extension
  because it accepts a precompiled binary from outside the deployment. An include is a text file under
  the same ownership check, edited by hand, and a pin on it would be stale after the next edit. An
  include that arrives from a package is what would reopen this.

<sub>See also [`config/an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight`](config.md#config-an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight), [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded), [`config/optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory`](config.md#config-optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory), [`config/a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in`](config.md#config-a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in).</sub>

<a id="config-an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight"></a>

## An include cycle is refused with the chain named, and nesting past eight is refused as depth

`rule:config/an-include-cycle-is-refused-and-nesting-is-capped-at-eight`

An include tree that reaches a file already on the chain is refused with the whole chain named
(`E0606`), and nesting deeper than eight files is refused as depth under the same code — not as a
cycle, because it may not be one. An include tree eight files deep is one no operator can read whether
or not it ever closes.

A cycle is caught by **name, not by depth**: the trust check hands back the canonical path, so a ring
built out of symlinks closes on a file the resolver has already seen even though no two spellings on
the chain match. A lexical comparison would let that ring through until the depth cap caught it, and
report the wrong thing.

<sub>See also [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir), [`config/app-keys-are-canonicalized-before-matching`](config.md#config-app-keys-are-canonicalized-before-matching).</sub>

<a id="config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded"></a>

## The tree is one ordered stream, a later assignment wins, and every override is recorded with both origins

`rule:config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`

The tree flattens to a single sequence: for each `--config` file in order, that file's own keys, then
its includes depth-first in list order; then the next `--config` file. **A later assignment wins**,
which makes an include override the file that pulled it in — the base-plus-local shape, with the
include line at the point the operator wants overridden.

What replaces the within-file refusal across files is an obligation, not a permission: **every
override is recorded with both origins**, surfaced in the boot log and in full by `nvs config dump
--origin` ([`config/check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline`](config.md#config-check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline)). This is the whole of what makes
"later wins" acceptable in a file that grants capabilities; without the record it is the silent
shadowing the format rule refused INI for, and a reader that drops the override list has removed a
security property, not a log line.

The override record is per key. Two files setting different keys of one block both survive, and a
partly written block keeps every unwritten key's default independently.
[`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one) keeps its scope: the same key twice
in *one* file is still refused.

- **Memory:** a live snapshot keeps one origin, a file and a line, for each directive set, plus the
  list of overrides. It is bounded by the number of directives, never by traffic, and the tree is
  parsed at boot and on each reload, never on the request path.

**Declined:**
- **Refusing every cross-file duplicate, so that an include may only add keys no other file set.** A
  host-local file could then never override a base default, only fill a gap the base left open, and
  that removes the reason to split files at all. Recording the override is what makes it safe instead.

<sub>See also [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`config/a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends`](config.md#config-a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends), [`config/check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline`](config.md#config-check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline), [`config/every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first`](config.md#config-every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first).</sub>

<a id="config-a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends"></a>

## A value array is replaced wholesale by a later file; `[[table]]` entries accumulate across the tree

`rule:config/a-value-array-replaces-and-a-table-appends`

`key = [...]` is one value, and a later value wins — so `[debug] mode`, `[capabilities] script.spawn`
and `debug.trace` are **replaced wholesale** by a later file. `[[extension]]`, `[[schedule]]`,
`[[server.mount]]`, `[[app]]` and `[[include]]` entries **accumulate** across the tree.

The split is not a special case: it is what each shape already means inside one file. Two
`[[schedule]]` blocks in one file are two schedules, so appending across files extends a rule rather
than adding one, and replacing would make the cross-file behaviour of the syntax differ from its
within-file behaviour. For a capability the direction also matters on its own: replacement means **the
last file that mentions a grant states the whole grant**, and no reader has to assemble the effective
root list from four files to know what it is.

A third array shape that fits neither half is the thing that would reopen this.

<sub>See also [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded), [`config/lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables`](config.md#config-lists-are-arrays-and-repeated-records-are-arrays-of-tables), [`config/every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first`](config.md#config-every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first).</sub>

<a id="config-a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in"></a>

## A relative path resolves against the directory of the file it is written in; a command-line path against the working directory

`rule:config/a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in`

Every path-valued directive — `opcache.file_cache_dir`, `capabilities.script.spawn`, `debug.trace`,
`[[extension]] path`, `[[server.mount]] root`, `[db.<name>] path`, `[storage.<name>] root`, `password_file`, an `[[app]]`
block's `root` or `entry`, `[[schedule]] script`, `[log] handler`, and `[[include]]`'s own `path` and `dir` — resolves relative to the
directory of the file the value appears in. A path given on the **command line** resolves against the
working directory, because that is what a shell argument means.

```toml
# /etc/nvs/nvs.toml
[[include]]
path = "conf.d/db.toml"            # -> /etc/nvs/conf.d/db.toml

# /etc/nvs/conf.d/db.toml
[db.main]
path = "data/app.sqlite"           # -> /etc/nvs/conf.d/data/app.sqlite
```

One rule shared with `[[include]]`, and the only one under which a configuration directory survives
being copied or relocated whole. The resolved absolute path is what the boot log and `nvs config dump`
print, so the rule never has to be applied in a reader's head — and a block in an included file names
a database beside *that* file, not beside the running program. A scheduled script and a log handler
are resolved while the configuration is read, so every fire and every escalation runs the same file
whatever folder the server was started in, and a schedule's boot check against the `script.spawn`
grant reads the same path each fire runs. Each is joined once per configuration read, and nothing on
the request path pays for it. A `[storage.<name>] root` is a folder the runtime joins an
object key to and opens through the same doors as a program's own paths, so left relative, every
object on the disk would meet the run-time refusal of a relative path
([`programs/relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file`](programs.md#programs-relative-paths-resolve-from-their-file)).

**Declined:**

- **Resolving a scheduled script or a log handler when it fires, against the file that wrote it.**
  The map of which file wrote each value would have to travel with the published configuration to
  every fire, and the boot log would still print the relative text.

<sub>See also [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir), [`config/app-keys-are-canonicalized-before-matching`](config.md#config-app-keys-are-canonicalized-before-matching), [`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value).</sub>

<a id="config-any-file-in-the-tree-may-set-any-directive"></a>

## Any file in the tree may set any directive, `System` class included

`rule:config/any-file-in-the-tree-may-set-any-directive`

Because [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary) is uniform, **any file in the tree may set any
directive**, `System` class included: capabilities, `[limits.hard]`, `[mode] ceiling` and
`[[extension]]` entries are as legitimate in `conf.d/host.toml` as in the root file, and a capability
grant in an included file takes effect.

Whoever can write an included file cleared exactly the same bar as whoever can write the root file, so
a rule restricting what an include may say would buy no security an attacker does not already have,
while costing per-host capability sets and per-environment extension sets. Confining `System`
directives to the root, or letting an include only narrow, would each invert deny-by-default at the
file layer: the root would have to grant every right any environment needs so that each host could
take some away.

<sub>See also [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded), [`config/system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it`](config.md#config-system-means-a-request-may-not-set-it).</sub>

<a id="config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary"></a>

## Every file the configuration reads, and its directory, must be owned by the runtime account or root and writable by nobody else

`rule:config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`

**Every file the configuration reads must be owned by the account the runtime runs as or by root, and
must not be group- or world-writable.** Its containing directory must pass the same check, ownership
included and not only the mode: an entry can be replaced by whoever can write the directory holding
it, whatever the file's own bits say. A failure is a refusal to start (`E0607`), naming the path and
the mode, and it is re-run on every reload. Its help is the one command that repairs that failure,
with the path, the owner or the group's SID filled in: `chown` or `chmod go-w` on Unix, and on
Windows `icacls /setowner *S-1-5-32-544` for an owner or `/inheritance:d` and `/remove:g <SID>` for a
group. The help is built only for a breach, so a path that passes costs nothing more.

**The directory that holds each link on the path as given is checked too.** A reload reads a root
through its links again ([`config/the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored`](config.md#config-the-resolved-root-is-announced-and-stored)), so whoever can write
the directory a link sits in chooses the file the next reload reads. Every prefix of the path that is a
link has its parent checked, a `current` link above the file as well as the file's own link. A path
with no link is checked as the file and its directory alone. A link's directory has one waiver the
file's directory lacks: **a root-owned directory on a read-only mount skips the mode test.** That is
the kubelet's ConfigMap volume, measured on `kind`: `0777 root:root` on a read-only `ext4` mount,
holding `override.toml -> ..data/override.toml` and `..data -> ..<timestamp>`. No account in the pod
can write it, and only root on the node changes it. A directory another account owns, or one on a
writable mount, keeps the mode test. The waiver is `trust::platform::check_link_holder`.

The configuration grants capabilities, so whoever can write any file in the tree can grant themselves
every one of them, and a running server publishes a saved file without a restart. The cache directory
already gets this refusal, and a file that grants `process.exec` cannot have less protection than a
directory of compiled code.

**On Windows the equivalent is the DACL**: the owner is the runtime account, `BUILTIN\Administrators`
or `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`, and no *effective* write right — data, append, EA, attributes, `DELETE`,
`WRITE_DAC` or `WRITE_OWNER` — reaches `Everyone`, `Authenticated Users`, `BUILTIN\Users`,
`BUILTIN\Guests` or `ANONYMOUS LOGON`. The two ACL rights are in the mask because either one buys all
the others in a second step. Effective rights rather than the presence of an ACE, so a deny entry
counts and an inherited grant is seen. Windows grants `Authenticated Users` modify rights by default on a non-system drive's
root, so a configuration kept under such a path refuses until that inheritance is broken — that default
*is* the hole this rule closes.

**On Unix, a file or directory on a read-only mount passes the owner test**: `statvfs` reports
`ST_RDONLY` for its file system. No account on this host can change it through that mount, and that
is the whole of what the owner test guards. A container's `-v ./app:/app:ro` is exactly this case:
the files belong to the host's account, which is not the container's, and refusing them would refuse
the deployment the Docker guide teaches. The mode test still runs there, so a group- or
world-writable mode on a read-only mount is refused: the mode says the tree is meant to be shared,
and the same tree mounted read-write later would be served. A path whose mount cannot be asked keeps
the owner test. Windows has no read-only mount to waive.

Docker Desktop on Windows can report a bind mount's files as `0777`, whatever the NTFS ACL says, and
then the mode test refuses them even under `:ro`. The guide tells a Windows user to copy the
configuration into the image instead. The mode test is not waived for it: a mode is the only answer
the container can read, and a check that trusted `0777` would trust every mount.

**One directory is checked without its parent: the default data folder**, `.nvsdata` beside the
running binary. Its parent is the binary's own directory, and an account that can write there can
already replace the binary, so examining it guards nothing the binary does not — while on a stock
Windows drive it would make the default folder unusable everywhere. A folder `--data` names, and every
path the configuration names, keeps the full check, parent included. A file inside the data folder is
checked as any file is, with the private data folder as its directory. Novis creates the data folder
private to its account and never re-permissions one that exists: it checks it.

**The account is a value the check takes, not one it reads.** `nvs serve` judges for its own account,
and a command that sets up or reports on a service judges for the account the service runs as, through
the same function: `trust::check_as` with a `trust::Account`, a uid on Unix and a SID on Windows. On
Unix a number is a uid and a name comes from the password database. On Windows `LocalSystem` is the
well-known SID, `NT SERVICE\<name>` is computed as Windows computes it (`S-1-5-80-` and the SHA-1 of
the upper-case name in UTF-16LE), because that account does not resolve until the service exists, and
any other name goes through `LookupAccountNameW`. A breach for a named account names it: "neither the
account `LocalSystem` nor an administrative one". `resolve::JudgedFor` resolves a tree that way.

**Declined:**
- **The full check on the default data folder.** It is correct in principle and unusable on a stock
  Windows drive, and it protects only against an account that could replace the binary anyway.
- **Waiving the mode test on a read-only mount too.** A writable mode under `:ro` is either a
  mistake or Docker Desktop's `0777`, and the container cannot tell the two apart. Only a
  root-owned directory that holds a link has that waiver, because a ConfigMap volume is exactly that.
- **The mode test on a link's directory with no waiver.** It refuses every Kubernetes ConfigMap,
  whose volume directory is `0777 root:root` on a read-only mount.
- **The waiver for a link's directory another account owns.** Docker Desktop's `0777` bind mount
  belongs to the host's account, and that is the case the mode test is kept for.
- **A configuration key that turns the check off.** It would be written in the file the check
  guards, so whoever can write the file could turn it off.

Where the check runs is [`config/the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered`](config.md#config-the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered).

<sub>See also [`config/optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory`](config.md#config-optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory), [`config/any-file-in-the-tree-may-set-any-directive`](config.md#config-any-file-in-the-tree-may-set-any-directive), [`config/the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered`](config.md#config-the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered), [`config/a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure`](config.md#config-a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure).</sub>

<a id="config-the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered"></a>

## The ownership check runs on `nvs serve`, on reload and in `config check --as` for the serving account; `nvs run`, plain `config check` and `config dump` read without it, and an unchecked file can grant nothing

`rule:config/the-ownership-check-runs-where-it-can-be-answered`

The ownership check runs where its question can be answered: `nvs serve` and reload, on the host and
as the account that will serve, `nvs config check --as <account>`, which names that account, and
`nvs service install`, its `--dry-run` included, and `nvs service status`, for the account the service
runs as.
Three readers resolve the tree without it, each for a reason of its own.

`nvs run` executes a program the invoking account named, from a working directory that account chose,
as that account: whoever can write its `./nvs.toml` can write the program, so the file adds no
authority the check would take away, and the Windows default would otherwise refuse nearly every
checkout. The data folder's `nvs.toml` read at step 3 is the same account's file, in a folder Novis
created private to it. Plain `nvs config check` and `nvs config dump` run on the auditing machine as
the auditing account, where the check answers a different question than the one it exists for — it
refuses trees the server would accept and passes trees the server would refuse, and a green result
that means neither is worse than one that does not claim to have looked.

**`nvs config check --as <account>` asks the question for the account that will serve.** It resolves
through `resolve::JudgedFor`, whose `trust` is `trust::check_as`, the function `nvs serve`'s boot runs,
so it stops at the same first file with the same `E0607` and help. On Unix the account is a user name
or a uid; on Windows a name, `LocalSystem`, or `NT SERVICE\<service>`, computed before the service
exists. A name this machine cannot resolve is `E0662`, before any file is read. `--as` judges the files
on this machine as they are now. It does not see the server's own copy of the files, a container's
read-only mount, whose owner waiver applies only where that mount is, or a deploy step that changes an
owner. The check trusts no group but the administrators one, so the account's group membership does
not change its answer. `config dump` takes no `--as`: it lists keys, and `check` is the verdict.

**`nvs service install` asks it for the service's account before it changes anything.** Every
`--config` file the stored argv names resolves through the same `JudgedFor`, for `LocalSystem` or the
`--account` on Windows and for root or the `--account` user on Linux. The first file that account
would refuse is that `E0607`, from a dry run as from a real install, before the data folder is
prepared and before the service manager is asked for anything. A file that is not there yet is the
template the install writes, and is not judged. On Linux a path the install gives to root or the
account, with the directory that holds it, is judged as the install leaves it, so it passes. On
Windows an elevated install's data folder and the `nvs.toml` it writes there are owned by
`Administrators`, which every service account trusts, so they pass at boot.

The install stops on `E0607`, and no flag lets it go on: the check is the function `serve` runs at
every boot, on this host, for this account, so its answer is the boot's, and a service that cannot
start is never what the operator asked for. A configuration that does not resolve and an account that
does not exist (`E0654`) stop the install for the same reason. The unreadable-file check beside it only
warns, because a group or an ACL it does not read can still grant the read; the ownership check reads
everything it judges. `Manager::judged_for` has no default, so a new manager cannot skip the check.

**`nvs service status` asks it again for the installed service.** After the manager's state it judges
every `--config` file of the argv the platform holds, for the account the platform holds the service
under, through the same `JudgedFor`. A refused file is the boot's `E0607` and exits `1`. A file this
prompt cannot read is `E0605` as a warning, and the exit stays `0`: an unelevated prompt cannot read a
service's private folder, and that says nothing about who can change the file.

`nvs serve` checks every file it reads, every time it reads it: the root, each include, each secret
file and each `[[app]]` fold a request or a queue job asks for, at boot and at every reload. A boot
that finds a file another account can write stops with `E0607` naming it; a reload that finds one is
refused, names the path in the log, and the running snapshot keeps serving. Development mode is
checked too. The mode is written in the same file, so a check the mode could skip is one whoever
writes the file could skip.

A Windows checkout on a non-system drive inherits the drive's `Authenticated Users` write grant, and
on the CI runners `BUILTIN\Users`' right to create files in every folder, so the repository's own
servers fail there until both are removed. `bun nv checkout-acl` removes them once, and CI's Windows
jobs run it before they build.

Two writes are checked even where the read is not: the data folder before anything is created in it,
and the directory a project command or `nvs init` writes the shipped `nvs.toml` into.

**What the exemption may never do is grant.** A capability or a `System` directive read through an
unchecked file on the `run` path carries the invoking account's own authority and nothing more: an
`nvs.toml` can grant a CLI program nothing it could not take for itself, and the rule that places the
capability check is bound by that sentence.

**Declined:**
- **Skipping the check under `nvs serve` in development mode.** The mode comes from the checked file.
- **Naming `bun nv checkout-acl` in `E0607`'s help.** The help is read by people who run Novis, not
  by people who work on it, and its `icacls` steps already fix a checkout.
- **A flag that installs past a failing check.** It installs a service that cannot start.
- **The check in `nvs service unit`.** It prints a definition for review, often on a machine that is
  not the server, and `install --dry-run` is the check on the host.
- **Listing every failing file, rather than the first.** `serve` stops at the first, and the
  pre-flight names the file the boot would name. A later change, if operators ask.

<sub>See also [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), [`config/check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline`](config.md#config-check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline), [`security/capability-question-is-grant-and-scope`](security.md#security-capability-question-is-grant-and-scope).</sub>

<a id="config-optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory"></a>

## `optional = true` covers absence and nothing else, and an absent include is checked at the directory that would hold it

`rule:config/optional-covers-absence-and-moves-the-check-to-the-directory`

**`optional = true` covers absence and nothing else.** A file that exists but cannot be read, that fails
the ownership check, or that fails to parse is a hard refusal — otherwise a stray `chmod` silently drops
half a configuration and the server comes up looking healthy.

Because an absent file offers nothing to check, **the check falls on the directory that would contain
it**:

```console
E0607: [[include]] /etc/nvs/local.toml is optional, but /etc/nvs is group-writable
       (mode 0775, group `deploy`)
       an absent optional include is a standing slot that anyone able to write that
       directory may later fill with root-owned configuration
       fix: chmod 0755 /etc/nvs
```

That refusal is the whole security argument for the feature. An optional include is a promise that a
file which does not exist yet will be trusted when it appears; the only place to make that promise
safely is the directory, and it is the one place a check can still run. When that directory does not
exist either, the check walks up to the nearest ancestor that does: the promise is only as strong as
the shallowest directory an attacker would have to write in order to keep it. A `dir` include's
directory is checked the same way.

<sub>See also [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary), [`config/include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir`](config.md#config-include-takes-a-path-or-a-dir).</sub>

<a id="config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value"></a>

## A secret directive has a `_file` sibling, exactly one of the pair is set, and the file's whole content is the value

`rule:config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`

A directive the registry marks **secret** — `[db.<name>] password`, `[mail.<name>] password`,
`[ldap.<name>] password`, `[http.client.proxy] password`, `[http] csrf_key` and `[cache.shared] password` —
gains a `_file` sibling. Exactly one of the pair may be set; both is a refusal, so this is two sources
for one value rather than a second spelling. The registry is one table, one row per pair, and a
credential on the typed tree with no row fails a census rather than parsing and never being read.

```toml
[db.main]
driver = "postgres"
password_file = "/run/secrets/db_password"
```

**The file's entire content is the value**, with exactly one trailing `\n` — and a `\r` immediately
before it — stripped if present, and nothing else trimmed. A password may legitimately begin or end
with a space, and removing it is [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)'s failure of repairing input
instead of reading it; an edge space is reported as a warning and kept. One newline goes because
`echo secret > f` produces one; a value that genuinely ends in a newline is written with two. The
content must be valid UTF-8, and an empty file, a whitespace-only file, or one over 64 KiB is refused
(`E0608`).

Only the `password_file` that won the merge is opened. The value never enters the merged table, is
never logged, and `nvs config dump` renders it `<secret>` beside the file it came from —
`password_file` stays set so the dump can name it. `Core\Config::all` renders every secret directive
`<secret>` too, whether a file or the tree set it, because a page or a log line that prints every
setting is the usual way a credential leaks. `Core\Config::get` returns the value: it is the one
reader a program that connects with the credential needs.

**`[secrets]` and `[app.secrets]` take the same pair** for every name the operator writes there:
`name` or `name_file`, exactly one, read by the same reader under the same rules. Their values are
`Core\Config::secret`'s and never `get`'s
([`config/settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values`](config.md#config-settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values)).

**`get` returns a secret directive as a `?secret string`, and only by its written name.** The
checker types `Core\Config::get('db.main.password')` as `?secret string` when the literal is a
secret directive, read from the same table the boot fills them from, so no output, log or
serialiser takes the value ([`security/secret-sinks-refuse`](security.md#security-secret-sinks-refuse)). Every other directive stays a
`?string`. A name the program computes cannot be typed by its value, so `get` throws `LogicError`
when a computed name turns out to be a secret directive: its result would otherwise be a plain
`?string` any sink takes. A method reference to `get` is a computed name too. **What it spends:**
one walk of the secret rows per `get`, and one word the compiler passes beside the name.

**Declined:**
- **A `secret` return for every `get`.** Most settings are a size, a duration or a level a program
  prints and compares, and every one of them would need a conversion.
- **A computed secret name answered `null`.** It reads as "not configured", which is the one fact a
  program checks before it connects, and it would be wrong.
- **Decrypting SOPS, `age` or a KMS envelope inside the binary**, so that a directive could name an
  encrypted file. It does not compose with the format: SOPS has no TOML store, so an encrypted
  configuration would be one opaque blob ahead of the merge, the includes and the dump. It puts the
  key that unlocks every credential into the process that compiles a program and parses hostile bytes,
  where today that process holds one plaintext credential. And it adds nothing: `sops -d`, a Vault
  agent, Sealed Secrets and a Kubernetes secret volume all end in a file, which a `_file` sibling
  reads unchanged. A deployment target that cannot produce a file at all is what would reopen this.
- **A `_file` sibling for every string directive.** It doubles the key space of the format and
  complicates the unknown-key refusal, to serve the handful of directives the registry marks.
- **An `_env` sibling, a third source naming an environment variable** (`password_env =
  "DB_PASSWORD"`). It is the narrow form of interpolation: it cannot grant, and it serves a platform
  that injects credentials only as variables. It still puts the credential where every child process
  inherits it and `/proc/<pid>/environ` and a crash dump show it, so `process.exec` would owe a scrub,
  and it serves no target that cannot also mount a file. The trigger above reopens it too.

<sub>See also [`config/a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure`](config.md#config-a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure), [`config/a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in`](config.md#config-a-relative-path-resolves-against-the-file-it-is-written-in), [`config/check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline`](config.md#config-check-and-dump-audit-the-tree-offline), [`security/secret-qualifier`](security.md#security-secret-qualifier), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused).</sub>

<a id="config-a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure"></a>

## A secret file another account can write refuses the boot; one another account can read only warns

`rule:config/a-secret-file-is-checked-for-integrity-and-advised-on-exposure`

A secret file is a configuration input like any other, so it passes
[`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary) before it is read: **group- or world-writable is a
refusal**, since another account able to rewrite the file chooses the credential the server connects
with.

Group- or world-*readable* is a warning naming the mode, not a refusal. Docker Compose mounts secrets
`0444` and Kubernetes secret volumes default to `0644`; inside a container that is the norm, on a
shared host it is not, and nothing readable from the runtime says which one it is in. Refusing would
wall off every containerised deployment; saying nothing would hide a real mistake on a shared host.
**Integrity is enforced; confidentiality is advised.** The advisory is printed in full by `nvs config
check` and counted on its summary line, and it never changes the verdict.

<sub>See also [`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary).</sub>

<a id="config-settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values"></a>

## `[settings]` and `[secrets]` hold a program's own values, read with `Core\Config::setting` and `Core\Config::secret`  *(designed — owned by goal app-settings)*

`rule:config/settings-and-secrets-are-a-programs-own-values`

Four blocks hold values a program reads by a name the operator chooses: `[settings]` and `[secrets]`
for every application, and `[app.settings]` and `[app.secrets]` under an `[[app]]` block for that
application. They are the only open blocks. Every other block stays closed, and an unknown key there
is still `E0601`.

```toml
[settings]
page_size = 20

[settings.api]
base = "https://api.example.com"

[secrets]
api_key_file = "/run/secrets/api_key"
```

**A key is a plain name**, `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`, at every depth. A sub-table adds a dotted
level, so `[settings.api] base` is read as `api.base`. A quoted key that is not a plain name is
`E0601`, because `"api.base"` and `[settings.api] base` would be two settings read by one name.

**A setting keeps its TOML type**: a string is a `string`, an integer an `int`, a float a `float`, a
boolean a `bool`, an array an array, and a table an array keyed by name. A TOML date or time is
`E0601`, and its help is the same value quoted as a string. Novis has no value a TOML date maps to
without a time-zone choice, and a string leaves that choice to the program.

**A secret is a string, written inline or read from a file.** Each `[secrets]` key is `name = "…"`
or `name_file = "…"`, exactly one of the two, and both is `E0608`, as for a secret directive
([`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value)). The file is read by the same reader,
under the same rules. A secret that is not a string is `E0601`, so `[secrets]` has no sub-table and
a secret's own name never ends in `_file`. Every value is carried beside the merged table under
`secrets.<name>` and never in it: the table keeps only the `_file` half, so `nvs config dump` prints
each secret as `<secret>` beside the file it came from. An inline secret names the configuration
file it was written in.

The key checks and the type checks run per file, before the merge, so a refusal names the line.
`[[include]]` overrides a value as it overrides any directive, and `[app.settings]` and
`[app.secrets]` fold over the global blocks key by key, least-specific first
([`config/every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first`](config.md#config-every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first)). Both record the override with
both origins ([`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded)). That is how one machine sets
its own values: the base file holds the defaults, and a file on that machine overrides them.

**Two read-only methods, and nothing else in the API:**

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `Core\Config::setting(string $name): ?(string\|int\|float\|bool\|array<mixed>)` | the value with its type, or `null` when no block sets it |
| `Core\Config::secret(string $name): ?secret string` | the secret, or `null` when no block sets it |

A program converts a setting with `as`: `Core\Config::setting('page_size') as int` throws when the
value is missing or is not a whole number. `secret`'s name is a sink, as `Core\Env::secret`'s is, so
a request cannot choose which secret it reads. A setting is not `tainted`: the operator wrote it in
a file only the runtime account or root may change. That is why `setting` returns a union of the
TOML types and not `mixed`: text out of `mixed` is `tainted` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)).
A table's values are `mixed`, so a program reads one untainted by its dotted name, `api.base`.

**`get`, `all`, `set` and `restore` never see the four blocks.** `Core\Config::get('secrets.x')`
returns `null`, and `all` lists no `settings.` or `secrets.` key. Without this, a secret would come
back from `get` as a plain `?string`, which every output accepts.

**A package reads the same values the application does**, as `Core\Env::secret` does not ask who
calls it. Which package may read what is the grants model's question
([`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time)).

**The typo check is a warning from `nvs config check`.** The checker records every name passed to
`setting` or `secret` as a literal string, per program. `nvs config check` compiles the programs the
tree names, each `[[app]] entry` and each `[[server.mount]]` entry, and every `--program <file>`
given, and raises `W1028` for each key in the four blocks that none of them reads. When any of them
passes a name that is not a literal, or a method reference to either method, no key is judged, and
one line says so. The same holds when a program does not compile or no program is named. One name
read by any program counts for every block, an `[[app]]` block's included. It is a warning because
a key may be read by a program the tree does not name. `nvs check` stays a source check that never
reads `nvs.toml` ([`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest)), and the boot compiles nothing
to look.

**What it spends.** A `setting` read is one lookup in the request's snapshot and one value built,
with nothing read from disk. The values are part of the config snapshot, stored once per snapshot
and never per request. A file that writes one of the four blocks is parsed once more at boot and at
each reload. `nvs config check` compiles each named program, which is seconds offline and nothing on
a server. Security: no capability can be set in the new blocks, every other block stays closed, and
a secret is typed `secret` and redacted wherever the configuration is printed.

**Declined:**
- **A free-form block with no declared keys and no typo check.** A typo'd key reads as "not set",
  which is the failure the unknown-key refusal exists to stop.
- **A schema the program declares, which the boot checks against.** `nvs.toml` is read before any
  program is compiled, and a schema would be source-tree state in a deployment file.
- **`${ENV}` interpolation into a setting**, already declined by
  [`config/the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml`](config.md#config-the-file-is-nvs-toml-and-it-is-toml).
- **Reading settings through `get` as strings.** Every value would need a parse, and a secret would
  come back as a plain string.
- **A `settings()` method that returns every value.** It is the way a whole set of secrets ends up
  in a log.
- **A `set` for settings.** A request that needs another value uses a variable.
- **A package that may not read the values.** A limit for these two methods would be a rule of its
  own, under the grants model.

<sub>See also [`config/every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added`](config.md#config-every-block-is-argued-where-it-is-added), [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value), [`config/every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first`](config.md#config-every-matching-app-block-applies-least-specific-first), [`config/later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded`](config.md#config-later-wins-and-every-override-is-recorded), [`config/ini-set-is-core-config-set`](config.md#config-ini-set-is-core-config-set), [`security/secret-has-no-ambient-source`](security.md#security-secret-has-no-ambient-source).</sub>

<a id="config-one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set"></a>

## The boot path and `Core\Config::set` parse a value through one implementation

`rule:config/one-parser-for-the-boot-path-and-config-set`

A value written in the file and a value handed to `Core\Config::set` go through **one parser**. Every
shipped default parses identically through the boot path and through `set`, and the two refusals the
boot makes — a value that is not a quantity, a name no directive governs — are the same two `set`
answers `false` with. A depth written as a bare integer and one written as `"64"` are the same value
wherever they arrive.

This is the shape [`expressions/preparation-preserves-behaviour`](expressions.md#expressions-preparation-preserves-behaviour) already establishes: a prepared
